So what makes an interval wide? Three things. First, the confidence you ask for. Take one sample of two hundred, and build its interval at eighty, ninety, ninety-five and ninety-nine percent. Each is wider than the last, from two point one to four point two five. More confidence costs precision. Second, the sample size. Hold the level at ninety-five, and grow the sample from twenty-five to sixteen hundred. Each time the data quadruples, the width roughly halves: eleven, five, two point three, one point two. And third, the spread of the data. Double it, and the width doubles too. The same recipe works for a rate.

Say five hundred and forty of three thousand visitors convert. That's eighteen percent. A rate's standard error comes from the rate itself, and here it's seven tenths of a point. Step one point nine six of those either way, and you get sixteen point six to nineteen point four percent. And an interval can answer a question you might think needs a test.

Build an interval for a difference. If it leaves out zero, the difference is significant at the five percent level. This one runs from minus a half to eight. It includes zero, so you can't rule out no effect. But it includes eight as well, a big effect you can't rule out either. That isn't proof of nothing. It's a call for more data. An interval and a test are two views of one thing, and only the interval shows how big the effect might be. Every interval so far leaned on a formula for the standard error.
